expectedText:
RESTRICTIONS ON EMPLOYER INQUIRY INTO ARREST, DIVERSION, AND SEALED CONVICTION RECORDS (LABOR CODE § 432.7) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Labor Code § 432.7 and § 432.8 — the state statutes restricting when Acme, Inc. may ask about, seek, or use information concerning an arrest that did not result in conviction, a referral to or participation in a pretrial or posttrial diversion program, or a conviction that has been judicially dismissed or ordered sealed, in connection with Jordan Lee's application for or employment in the position of Warehouse Associate, together with Section 432.8's separate rule for certain marijuana-related convictions more than two years old. This corpus separately includes a California Fair Chance Act ('Ban the Box') — Information Sheet, which describes the related but distinct restriction on inquiring into conviction history before a conditional offer of employment, and which cross-references Section 432.7 for certain definitions and for one of its own narrow exceptions without independently quoting Section 432.7's own text. This document focuses instead on Section 432.7 and Section 432.8 themselves — what those statutes state an employer may not ask, seek, use, or disclose; the exceptions the statutes state; and the remedies the statutes describe. It states facts about what these statutes require. It is not itself a job application, a background-check report, or any notice, and it does not tell Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee what to do about any particular arrest record, conviction, application, or employment decision.

THE CORE PROHIBITION: ARREST NOT RESULTING IN CONVICTION, DIVERSION PROGRAMS, AND DISMISSED OR SEALED CONVICTIONS
California Labor Code § 432.7 states that an employer — a public agency, private individual, or corporation — may not ask an applicant for employment to disclose, in writing or verbally, information concerning an arrest or detention that did not result in a conviction, a referral to or participation in a pretrial or posttrial diversion program, or a conviction that has been judicially dismissed or ordered sealed pursuant to law. The statute separately states that an employer may not seek that same category of information from any other source, or utilize it as a factor in determining hiring, promotion, termination, or admission to an apprenticeship or other training program leading to employment. The statute's own text carves out one item from this prohibition: it states that the section does not prevent an employer from asking an applicant or employee about an arrest for which that person is out on bail or on their own recognizance pending trial.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer, whether a public agency or private individual or corporation, shall not ask an applicant for employment to disclose, through any written form or verbally, information concerning an arrest or detention that did not result in conviction, or information concerning a referral to, and participation in, any pretrial or posttrial diversion program, or concerning a conviction that has been judicially dismissed or ordered sealed pursuant to law, including, but not limited to, Sections 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.425, 1203.45, and 1210.1 of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, restriction on employer inquiries into arrest, diversion, and dismissed or sealed conviction records (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  "An employer also shall not seek from any source whatsoever, or utilize, as a factor in determining any condition of employment including hiring, promotion, termination, or any apprenticeship training program or any other training program leading to employment, any record of arrest or detention that did not result in conviction, or any record regarding a referral to, and participation in, any pretrial or posttrial diversion program, or concerning a conviction that has been judicially dismissed or ordered sealed pursuant to law, including, but not limited to, Sections 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.425, 1203.45, and 1210.1 of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, restriction on employer seeking or using the same information from any other source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  "This section shall not prevent an employer from asking an employee or applicant for employment about an arrest for which the employee or applicant is out on bail or on their own recognizance pending trial."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, statutory carve-out for arrests while out on bail or own recognizance pending trial (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general ask/seek/utilize prohibition in Labor Code § 432.7(a)(1) and its own bail/own-recognizance carve-out. It does not address the statute's separate juvenile-court-record prohibition in subdivision (a)(2), which covers arrest, detention, and court-disposition information arising from juvenile-court proceedings. This clause independently fetched and verified this text directly from the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) on two separate fetches using different browser identifications, both returning byte-identical section text; it does not rely on the cross-references to this section stated, without independent verification, in this corpus's other documents.

HOW THE STATUTE DEFINES "CONVICTION"
For purposes of Labor Code § 432.7, the statute defines "conviction" to include a plea, verdict, or finding of guilt, regardless of whether the court imposed a sentence. The statute separately states that "conviction," for this purpose, does not include, and is not to be construed to include, any adjudication by a juvenile court or any other court order or action taken with respect to a person who is under the process and jurisdiction of the juvenile court.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Conviction” includes a plea, verdict, or finding of guilt, regardless of whether a sentence is imposed by the court."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(a)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "conviction" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  "“Conviction” does not include, and shall not be construed to include, any adjudication by a juvenile court or any other court order or action taken with respect to a person who is under the process and jurisdiction of the juvenile court."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(a)(3)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, exclusion of juvenile-court adjudications from the definition of "conviction" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  Known gap: This clause independently verifies the definition of "conviction" in Labor Code § 432.7(a)(3) itself — the definition that this corpus's California Fair Chance Act — Information Sheet document cross-references, through Government Code § 12952(f)(1), without independently quoting Section 432.7's own text. This clause does not address Section 432.7's separate juvenile-record inquiry prohibition in subdivision (a)(2), which restricts inquiry into juvenile-court arrest, detention, and disposition information regardless of whether that proceeding resulted in what this subdivision defines as a "conviction."

EXCEPTIONS THE STATUTE STATES
Labor Code § 432.7 states several exceptions to its own restrictions. Subdivision (e) states that persons seeking employment or already employed as peace officers, and persons seeking employment with the Department of Justice or another criminal justice agency as defined in Penal Code § 13101, are not covered by the section at all. Subdivision (m) states that the prohibition on asking about or seeking information regarding a conviction does not prohibit an employer from asking an applicant about, or seeking, a "particular conviction" of the applicant — regardless of whether that conviction has been expunged, judicially ordered sealed, statutorily eradicated, or judicially dismissed following probation — in any of several circumstances stated by the statute: where a federal or state law requires the employer to obtain that information; where the position sought would require the applicant to possess or use a firearm; where a law prohibits a person with that conviction from holding the position sought; or where a law prohibits the employer from hiring an applicant who has that conviction. The statute defines a "particular conviction," for purposes of this exception, as a conviction for specific criminal conduct or a category of criminal offenses that a federal or state law expressly bases requirements or exclusions on. Separately, subdivision (n) states that the section does not prohibit an employer that is required by state, federal, or local law to conduct criminal background checks, or to restrict employment based on criminal history, from complying with those requirements, and does not prohibit the employer from seeking or receiving a criminal history report obtained under procedures otherwise provided by federal, state, or local law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Persons seeking employment or persons already employed as peace officers, or persons seeking employment in positions in the Department of Justice or other criminal justice agencies as defined in Section 13101 of the Penal Code are not covered by this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, exclusion of peace-officer and criminal-justice-agency positions from the section's coverage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  "Paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) does not prohibit an employer, whether a public agency or private individual or corporation, from asking an applicant about, or seeking from any source information regarding, a particular conviction of the applicant if, pursuant to Section 1829 of Title 12 of the United States Code or any other federal law, federal regulation, or state law, any of the following apply:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(m)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "particular conviction" exception, introductory clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  "The employer is required by law to obtain information regarding the particular conviction of the applicant, regardless of whether that conviction has been expunged, judicially ordered sealed, statutorily eradicated, or judicially dismissed following probation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(m)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "particular conviction" exception where the employer is legally required to obtain the information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  "The applicant would be required to possess or use a firearm in the course of their employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(m)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "particular conviction" exception for positions requiring possession or use of a firearm (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  "For purposes of this subdivision, “particular conviction” means a conviction for specific criminal conduct or a category of criminal offenses prescribed by any federal law, federal regulation, or state law that contains requirements, exclusions, or both, expressly based on that specific criminal conduct or category of criminal offenses."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(m)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "particular conviction" for purposes of the subdivision (m) exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  "This section does not prohibit an employer, whether a public agency or private individual or corporation, required by state, federal, or local law to conduct criminal background checks for employment purposes or to restrict employment based on criminal history from complying with those requirements, or to prohibit the employer from seeking or receiving an applicant’s criminal history report that has been obtained pursuant to procedures otherwise provided for under federal, state, or local law."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(n) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, exception for employers legally required to conduct criminal background checks (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  Known gap: This clause independently verifies the peace-officer/criminal-justice-agency exclusion in subdivision (e)(1), the "particular conviction" exceptions in subdivision (m), and the legally-required-background-check exception in subdivision (n). It does not address subdivision (e)(2)'s narrower rule for nonsworn criminal-justice-agency employees, subdivision (f)'s exception for certain health-facility employer inquiries (referenced, but not independently quoted, in this corpus's Fair Chance Act — Information Sheet document, and not independently verified by this clause either), or subdivisions (g) through (l), which address law-enforcement recordkeeping restrictions and public-agency concessionaire screening — subjects distinct from a private employer's own hiring inquiry. This clause does not determine whether any specific position, employer, or conviction falls within any of these statutory exceptions.

SEPARATE TREATMENT OF CERTAIN OLD MARIJUANA-RELATED CONVICTIONS
A separate Labor Code section, § 432.8, extends the limitations on employers and the penalties stated in § 432.7 to a conviction for violating specific marijuana-related provisions of the Health and Safety Code — subdivision (b) or (c) of § 11357 (or a statutory predecessor), subdivision (c) of § 11360, or §§ 11364, 11365, or 11550 as those sections related to marijuana before January 1, 1976 (or a statutory predecessor) — once two years have passed from the date of that conviction. As currently published on the California Legislative Information website, Section 432.8 was added to the Labor Code in 1976 and has not been further amended since.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The limitations on employers and the penalties provided for in Section 432.7 shall apply to a conviction for violation of subdivision (b) or (c) of Section 11357 of the Health and Safety Code or a statutory predecessor thereof, or subdivision (c) of Section 11360 of the Health and Safety Code, or Section 11364, 11365, or 11550 of the Health and Safety Code as they related to marijuana prior to January 1, 1976, or a statutory predecessor thereof, two years from the date of such a conviction."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.8 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, extension of Section 432.7's limitations and penalties to certain marijuana-related convictions after two years (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.8.)
  Known gap: This clause independently fetched and verified Labor Code § 432.8 directly as its own statutory section — it is a separate section from § 432.7, not a subdivision within it, though it operates by cross-reference to Section 432.7's limitations and penalties. Section 432.8's rule is narrower than a blanket "any marijuana conviction over two years old" rule: it applies only to convictions under the specific Health and Safety Code provisions the statute lists (or their statutory predecessors), not to every marijuana-related offense. This clause does not determine whether any particular conviction falls within one of those listed provisions or their statutory predecessors, which is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve, and it does not address how other, more recent California cannabis-legalization and record-relief statutes may separately affect older marijuana convictions.

REMEDIES THE STATUTE STATES
Labor Code § 432.7 states its own civil and criminal remedies for a violation. If a person violates the section, or the separate Penal Code provisions on dissemination of criminal history information beginning at Penal Code § 11140, the statute states that the applicant may bring an action to recover actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees. For an intentional violation, the statute states that the applicant may recover treble actual damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and that an intentional violation is also a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500. The statute states that these remedies are in addition to, and not in place of, any other rights and remedies an applicant may have under other law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If a person violates this section, or Article 6 (commencing with Section 11140) of Chapter 1 of Title 1 of Part 4 of the Penal Code, the applicant may bring an action to recover from that person actual damages or two hundred dollars ($200), whichever is greater, plus costs, and reasonable attorney’s fees. An intentional violation of this section shall entitle the applicant to treble actual damages, or five hundred dollars ($500), whichever is greater, plus costs, and reasonable attorney’s fees. An intentional violation of this section is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not to exceed five hundred dollars ($500)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, civil damages and misdemeanor penalty for a violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  "The remedies under this section shall be in addition to and not in derogation of all other rights and remedies that an applicant may have under any other law."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, remedies stated as cumulative with other law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.7.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the remedies and penalties that Labor Code § 432.7(c)-(d) itself describes. It does not address remedies or requirements that may separately arise under the Fair Chance Act (Government Code § 12952) or the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, both covered independently elsewhere in this corpus, and it does not address how a court would apply these remedy provisions to any particular set of facts, which is a legal conclusion this document does not draw.
